::: {.module-line .content-visible when-format="html"}
**Module 3** · 50 min · [Open the slides for this module](03-movement-slides.html)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Learning objectives"}
- Move an object in `update()`, scaled by `delta`.
- Read the keyboard with cursor keys and `addKeys`.
- Turn a sprite to face the way it moves.
- Keep an object on screen with `Clamp`.
:::

## Where you start

You have [stopping point A](02-first-scene.qmd#what-you-have): a floor, a freezer and a researcher who stands still. By the end of this lesson you can walk the researcher to a sample, pick it up, and carry it to the freezer.

Everything in this lesson happens in `update(time, delta)`, the method Phaser calls every frame.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
- `time` is how long the game has been running, in milliseconds.
- `delta` is how long the last frame took, in milliseconds: about 16.7 at 60 frames per second.

You'll use `delta` all the time and `time` rarely.
:::

## Move something

The smallest possible movement: slide the researcher right at 200 pixels per second.

```js
update(time, delta) {
  this.player.x += 200 * (delta / 1000);
}
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Save, and the researcher walks off the right edge of the screen. `200 * (delta / 1000)` is speed × seconds, so the distance per second is the same at any frame rate ([lesson 0](00-engine.qmd#frames-arent-all-the-same-length)).

`x` and `y` are plain properties: you can read them, change them, or set both with `setPosition(x, y)`.
:::

## Read the keyboard

Ask Phaser for keys once, in `create()`. Check them every frame, in `update()`.

```js
create() {
  // ...
  this.cursors = this.input.keyboard.createCursorKeys(); // up, down, left, right, space, shift
  this.wasd = this.input.keyboard.addKeys('W,A,S,D');     // { W, A, S, D }
}

update(time, delta) {
  if (this.cursors.right.isDown) {
    this.player.x += 200 * (delta / 1000);
  }
}
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Each key is an object, and `isDown` is `true` for every frame the key is held. For something that should happen once per press (open a menu, jump), use `Phaser.Input.Keyboard.JustDown(key)` instead: it's `true` only on the first frame.

Supporting both the arrows and WASD costs one line and saves left-handed players and laptop users a lot of grief.
:::

## Turn keys into a direction

Instead of four `if`s, turn the keys into a direction: `dx` is −1, 0 or 1, and so is `dy`.

```js
const k = this.cursors;
const w = this.wasd;
const dx = (k.right.isDown || w.D.isDown ? 1 : 0) - (k.left.isDown || w.A.isDown ? 1 : 0);
const dy = (k.down.isDown || w.S.isDown ? 1 : 0) - (k.up.isDown || w.W.isDown ? 1 : 0);
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Right gives `1 - 0 = 1`. Left gives `0 - 1 = -1`. Both at once cancel out to `0`, which is what you'd want. Remember that `y` grows **down**, so the down key is `+1`.
:::

## Diagonals are too fast

Holding right and down moves `1` along `x` **and** `1` along `y` each step. That's √2 ≈ 1.41 times as far as moving straight.

```js
const length = Math.hypot(dx, dy) || 1; // 1 for straight, 1.41 for diagonal, 0 → 1 when still
const step = (SPEED * delta) / 1000;
this.player.x += (dx / length) * step;
this.player.y += (dy / length) * step;
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Dividing by the length makes the direction a **unit vector**: length 1, whichever way it points. `|| 1` avoids dividing by zero when no key is down.

You'll meet `Phaser.Math.Vector2` in lesson 4, which does this for you with `.normalize()`. It's worth doing by hand once.
:::

## Face the way you walk

The researcher spritesheet has frames for facing down (1), up (5) and sideways (9). Sideways faces right, so flip it for left.

```js
if (dx !== 0) {
  this.player.setFrame(9).setFlipX(dx < 0);
} else if (dy !== 0) {
  this.player.setFrame(dy < 0 ? 5 : 1);
}
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`setFlipX(true)` mirrors the sprite left to right. It's free: one spritesheet covers both directions.

When no key is down, nothing changes, so the researcher keeps facing the last way they walked. It's a tiny thing that makes a character feel solid. Lesson 5 replaces single frames with walk animations.
:::

## Stay on the screen

```js
const { width, height } = this.scale;
this.player.x = Phaser.Math.Clamp(this.player.x, 32, width - 32);
this.player.y = Phaser.Math.Clamp(this.player.y, 32, height - 32);
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`Clamp(value, min, max)` keeps a number in a range. The 32 pixels of margin is half the researcher's size at `setScale(2)`, so they stop at the edge instead of halfway off it.

`Phaser.Math` is full of small helpers like this: `Between` (a random integer), `Distance.Between`, `Angle.Between`, `Linear` (interpolate). Check it before writing your own.
:::

## Pick up and carry

No physics yet, so "touching" means "close enough". Each frame, measure the distance to the sample and to the freezer.

{{< snippet file="stopping-points/stopB/src/scenes/Play.js" lines="62-77" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
While you carry the sample, it follows you: every frame, put it 44 pixels above the researcher's head. Close enough to the freezer, and the sample goes back to the rack and the counter goes up.

`this.carrying` is the first piece of **game state**: a value that decides what the game does next. Watch how much of the game ends up depending on values like this. Lesson 7 is about where they should live.
:::

To catch up, copy `stopping-points/stopB` and run it:

```bash
cp -r stopping-points/stopB my-cold-chain-b
cd my-cold-chain-b && npm install && npm run dev
```
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Walk over the freezer, though: the researcher is drawn on top of it, and walks straight through. Nothing in the game knows the freezer is solid. That's what physics is for, in lesson 4.
:::

## Going further: containers

A **container** groups game objects so they move, scale and rotate together. Instead of moving the tube by hand every frame, you could carry it in a container with the researcher:

```js
this.carrier = this.add.container(width / 2, height / 2);
this.carrier.add(this.player);           // positions inside are relative to the container
this.player.setPosition(0, 0);
// on pickup:
this.carrier.add(this.tube);
this.tube.setPosition(0, -44);
// in update(): move this.carrier instead of this.player
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Containers are handy for things that really are one object made of parts: a health bar with a frame and a fill, a cart with a box on it. *Cold Chain* doesn't use one for the player, because physics bodies (lesson 4) don't work well inside containers. Moving the tube by hand is simpler.
:::

```js
const SPEED = 200;

update(time, delta) {
  // ...dx and dy as in the lesson...
  this.player.x += dx * SPEED * delta;
  this.player.y += dy * SPEED * delta;
}
```

## Key points

- `update(time, delta)` runs every frame. Move things by *speed × `delta` / 1000*.
- Create keys once in `create()`. Check `isDown` every frame in `update()`, or `JustDown` for one-off presses.
- Turn keys into a direction, and divide by its length so diagonals aren't faster.
- `setFrame` and `setFlipX` make a sprite face the way it moves.
- Without physics, "touching" means checking distances yourself, and nothing is solid.

**Next:** [Lesson 4: Physics](04-physics.qmd)
